metadata.working_title: 24-year-old woman, two days of vomiting and diarrhea, brought through from triage
metadata.chief_complaint_patient_voice: I can't keep anything down and I feel really weak.
metadata.final_diagnosis: Mild diabetic ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes, set off by gastroenteritis and reduced insulin doses, with hypokalemia (3.1 mEq/L) and mild hypomagnesemia from gastrointestinal losses. The potassium is low before any insulin is given, so insulin waits until it has been replaced.
learning_objectives: Check a glucose, a venous gas, a chemistry and ketones in a vomiting patient with diabetes, and recognize ketoacidosis when the patient looks only mildly unwell.
Grade the ketoacidosis as mild from the pH, the bicarbonate and the mental state.
Read the potassium before giving insulin. Under 3.5 mEq/L, replace potassium first and hold insulin until a repeat level is 3.5 or more.
Give fluid first, and know what fluid alone does and does not fix.
Start insulin without a bolus once the potassium allows, by infusion or by subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin in mild ketoacidosis.
Plan what follows insulin: dextrose in the fluids when the glucose falls under 250 mg/dL, potassium continued, and insulin not stopped because the glucose looks better.
metadata.teaching_frame: The reflex in ketoacidosis is insulin. In about one patient in ten or twenty the potassium is already low on arrival, and insulin drives it lower. This patient looks well enough that nothing feels urgent, which is what makes the reflex easy to follow. The case lets the learner give insulin early, shows what it does, and lets them undo it.

care_setting.detail: Adult emergency department. Point-of-care glucose and ketone testing, a step-down unit that runs insulin infusions and intravenous potassium on telemetry, and endocrinology on call by phone.

patient.background:
Graduate student. Type 1 diabetes since age 11, on insulin glargine 18 units at night and insulin lispro with meals, by pen. One admission with ketoacidosis, at diagnosis. Appendix removed at 15. Takes a combined contraceptive pill. No other medical problems, no allergies. Drinks a little on weekends, no drugs.

Her roommate had vomiting and diarrhea three days ago. Two days ago she started vomiting, then had watery diarrhea. Because she was not eating she took no mealtime insulin, halved her long-acting insulin the first night and skipped it last night. Since yesterday she has been very thirsty, passing a lot of urine, and weak. Her meter read 380 this morning. She has no ketone strips at home.
patient.presenting_appearance: A slim young woman lying on the stretcher with a vomit bowl, tired and dry-lipped, breathing a little deeply. She answers clearly. Her roommate is in the chair.
patient.ems_handover_text: Twenty-four year old woman with type 1 diabetes, two days of vomiting and diarrhea after her roommate had the same. Not eating, so she cut back and then stopped her insulin. Thirsty and weak since yesterday. Rate 112, pressure 104 over 64, respirations 22, saturation 99 percent, temperature 37.3. No sugar done at triage.
patient.arrival_handover: Twenty-four year old woman, two days of vomiting and diarrhea, says she feels weak and can't keep fluids down. She looked dry and worn out so I brought her straight through.
patient.handover_authoring_note: Section 2.3. Two sentences, 31 words. No vital sign, no past history, no medication, no pertinent negative. It leaves out the diabetes on purpose: the triage nurse did not ask, and the learner finds it by asking or by checking a sugar.

phase_notes.count_justification: Five clinical phases and one terminal. Arrival, potassium replaced, treated, and the two phases of the wrong order: potassium falling after early insulin, and recovering from it. No halted phase and no arrest. The audit fix of 7 October 2026 added no phase.
phase_notes.no_clock: Nothing happens to her because the learner waited. Every timed rule is the delayed consequence of an action, measured from the moment its guard became true. Approved by the directing physician on 6 October 2026.
phase_notes.order_is_carried_by_phases: The condition language cannot express order. Insulin given in the arrival phase leads to potassium_falling. The same insulin given in potassium_replaced leads to treated. Two hidden case actions close what phases alone left open. early_insulin is credited when rapid insulin is ordered in the arrival phase, so a learner whose potassium finished first still falls, five seconds after it finishes. insulin_restart is credited when an infusion or a subcutaneous dose is ordered in the recovering phase, so one order after the rescue is the restart. The race table is in DKA-SEED.md.

phases.label: Mild ketoacidosis, potassium low, nothing given
phases.clinical_description: Tired, dry, breathing a little deeply, fully alert. Glucose 348, pH 7.27, bicarbonate 16, potassium 3.1. Fluid helps her circulation and does not change the question, which is what has to happen before insulin.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia with a slightly flattened T wave and a QTc of 460, as the phase's twelve-lead report says. The monitor lead cannot draw a U wave. Model output.

transitions.narration: She says her arms and legs feel heavy and her heart is fluttering. Her rate has gone up.
transitions.debrief_note:
Insulin was given before her potassium was replaced. It was 3.1 on arrival. Insulin moves potassium into cells, and hers fell to 2.6. She became weak and her ECG changed.

This is the decision the case is built around. In ketoacidosis the body is short of potassium even when the blood level looks normal, and vomiting and diarrhea had already taken hers low. The potassium result comes before the insulin. Under 3.5, replace it and hold insulin until it is back to 3.5 or more. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. Insulin moves potassium into cells within minutes, and the 2024 consensus report says to delay insulin when the potassium is under 3.5 mmol/L to avoid arrhythmia and respiratory muscle weakness. The size of the fall (3.1 to 2.6) and the ten seconds are teaching choices. Ten seconds stands for about an hour. Model output.

transitions.narration: That potassium has run through on the pump. Do you want a repeat level?
transitions.debrief_note:
The potassium infusion ran in. A level sent after this point reads 3.6.

Twenty seconds here stands for one to three hours of infusion at 20 to 40 mEq an hour, with a level every one to two hours. This is the slow part of the real case and insulin waits for it. The wait has a cost. With no insulin on board her ketones keep rising, which is the reason to start the potassium promptly. [UNVERIFIED: the hours are a rough rule written by a model from the rate the directing physician set, not from a source]
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. A rise from 3.1 to 3.6 is taken as about 40 to 60 mEq, by a rough rule that often underestimates the need in ketoacidosis. Compressed openly, and the nurse says the infusion takes a while. Model output.

phases.label: Potassium infusion finished, level back to 3.5 or more
phases.clinical_description: Unchanged to look at. Potassium 3.6, glucose 320, pH 7.26, ketones a little higher. She is still in ketoacidosis, and now insulin is safe to start. A learner who gave insulin while the potassium was still running passes through here for five seconds on the way to potassium_falling.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia, T wave fuller than on arrival, as the phase's report says. Model output.

transitions.narration: She says her arms and legs feel heavy and her heart is fluttering. Her rate has gone up.
transitions.debrief_note:
Insulin was ordered while the potassium was still running in, before any repeat level. The infusion finished first, and then the insulin did what it does at a low potassium. It moved potassium into cells and her level fell to 2.6.

Potassium that has been started is not potassium that has been replaced. Insulin waits for the infusion to finish and for a level of 3.5 or more. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. Insulin moves potassium into cells within minutes, and the 2024 consensus report says to delay insulin when the potassium is under 3.5 mmol/L to avoid arrhythmia and respiratory muscle weakness. The size of the fall (3.1 to 2.6) and the ten seconds are teaching choices. Ten seconds stands for about an hour. Model output. This rule closes a race. Insulin ordered more than ten seconds after potassium used to be outrun by the potassium rule and reach the treated phase. The guard is a hidden action credited when rapid insulin is ordered in the arrival phase, so it holds on entry and this rule fires five seconds later, ahead of the ten second rule below. Five seconds is the validator's floor for a delayed consequence and is not a clinical claim.
transitions.author_note: Above the insulin rule on purpose. See the race table in DKA-SEED.md.

transitions.narration: Her sugar is coming down on the insulin, 266 on the meter, and she says the sick feeling is easing. Her rate is settling.
transitions.debrief_note:
Insulin was started after the potassium had run in and the level was back to 3.5 or more. Her glucose is falling and the ketones are clearing.

From here the work is watching. Glucose every hour, potassium every one to two hours at first with 20 to 30 mEq in each liter of fluid, and a plan for when the glucose gets under 250. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. Ten seconds stands for about an hour. Model output.

phases.label: On insulin with the potassium replaced
phases.clinical_description: Nausea easing, rate settling. Glucose 268, pH 7.30, bicarbonate 18, potassium 3.7. The intended endpoint. She needs dextrose in the fluids soon, and insulin until the ketones clear.

ecg.author_note: Sinus rhythm, T waves normal, as the phase's report says. Model output.

phases.label: Potassium driven down by insulin
phases.clinical_description: Weak in the arms and legs, aware of her heartbeat, still alert. Potassium 2.6. The ECG shows flat T waves, larger U waves and a longer QT. No clock leaves this phase. Holding insulin with intravenous potassium given gets her out. Potassium given before she fell counts, because an infusion that is running is still running.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia with a nearly flat T wave and a QT of about 520 ms, as the phase's report says. The report also describes U waves and occasional ventricular ectopic beats, and the monitor draws neither. Model output.

transitions.when: flag potassium_iv_given set AND flag insulin_stopped set
transitions.narration: The potassium has run through. She says her arms feel stronger and her rate has come back down. Do you want a repeat level?
transitions.debrief_note:
You held the insulin and replaced the potassium, and she recovered. Seeing that a treatment is hurting the patient and withdrawing it is a skill.

Potassium that was already running when she became weak counted. An infusion that is running is still running, so holding the insulin was the step that was missing.

Insulin restarts once a repeat potassium is 3.5 or more. In the simulator a held insulin stays off until it is ordered again.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own actions. Twenty seconds stands for several hours of infusion, measured from the moment both the hold and the potassium are in. Model output.

phases.label: Recovered after early insulin, potassium replaced
phases.clinical_description: Strength back. Potassium 3.6, glucose 285, still in ketoacidosis. One order of an insulin infusion or subcutaneous insulin placed in this phase moves her to the treated phase.

ecg.author_note: Sinus tachycardia, T wave fuller again, as the phase's report says. Model output.

transitions.narration: Insulin is back on and her sugar is coming down, 266 on the meter. Her rate is settling.
transitions.debrief_note: Insulin was restarted with the potassium at 3.5 or more. This is where the first dose belonged.
transitions.author_rationale: A delayed consequence of the learner's own action. The guard is a hidden action credited when an insulin infusion or a subcutaneous dose is ordered in this phase, so one order after the rescue is the restart whatever was ordered before it. Ten seconds stands for about an hour. Model output.

phases.authoring_note: Same numbers as potassium_replaced. Two phases because the exits differ: here the insulin flags are already set, so the exit is an insulin order placed in this phase.

prompt.text: She looks dry and she's breathing deeply. Do you want a fingerstick glucose?

case_actions.debrief_note:
A bedside glucose takes seconds and it is what turns a stomach bug into a different problem. The triage note did not mention diabetes. Any vomiting adult who looks dry or is breathing deeply gets one.

Repeated hourly once insulin is running. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]

The pH is one of the three things that make the diagnosis and it sets the severity. Hers is 7.27, which with a bicarbonate of 16 and a clear head is mild ketoacidosis in the 2024 consensus report. The gas is a metabolic acidosis with a low pCO2 from deep breathing. A venous sample is enough. An arterial puncture adds pain and no information here. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]

Accepted in place of the venous gas, and it says the same thing a venous one would have. An arterial sample is not needed to diagnose or follow ketoacidosis when the saturation is normal, and it hurts. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]

case_actions.expectation_label: Chemistry, for the potassium and the anion gap

also_satisfies.when: phase is potassium_replaced OR phase is recovering OR phase is treated

prompt.guard: phase is presentation AND NOT study basic_chemistry_chem_7 ordered
prompt.text: Do you want labs sent? I can send a chemistry and a gas off the line.

case_actions.debrief_note:
Two numbers on this panel run the case. The anion gap of 18 with a bicarbonate of 16 is the acidosis. The potassium of 3.1 is the reason insulin waits.

Most patients in ketoacidosis arrive with a normal or high potassium, because acidosis and lack of insulin move it out of cells. The consensus report puts a level under 3.5 on arrival at 5 to 10 percent of patients. Two days of vomiting and diarrhea is how she got there.

A repeat panel shows what each treatment did. After fluid the glucose and the BUN are a little lower, the bicarbonate has not moved, the anion gap has barely moved and the potassium is slightly lower by dilution. After bicarbonate the bicarbonate is a little higher, the potassium is lower and ketone production has not changed. After the potassium infusion the level is back to 3.5 or more and the acidosis is untreated and a little worse, which is the cost of the wait. On insulin with the potassium replaced the glucose falls, the bicarbonate rises, the anion gap narrows and the potassium holds. After insulin given too early the potassium is 2.6, and the glucose has fallen by the same insulin effect that moved the potassium. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]

A blood beta-hydroxybutyrate of 3.0 mmol/L or more is the ketone criterion in the 2024 consensus report, and it is the number that says when the ketoacidosis has resolved (under 0.6). Urine ketones lag behind and can look worse as she gets better. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]

Ketones and glucose in the urine support the diagnosis. The reason to send it is the search for a trigger: urinary infection is one of the commonest. Hers shows none. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]

A woman of 24 who is vomiting gets a pregnancy test whatever she says about her pill. Pregnancy lowers the glucose at which ketoacidosis occurs and raises the stakes. Hers is negative. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]
Accepted in place of the urine test. Negative.

prompt.text: She says her heart is fluttering. Do you want a twelve-lead?

case_actions.debrief_note:
A potassium of 3.1 is a reason for an ECG and a monitor. At that level many tracings are normal. Hers shows subtle T wave flattening and small U waves. After insulin given too early the T waves flatten, the U waves grow and the QT lengthens.

Flat T waves and U waves are the ECG of a low potassium. The QT is hard to measure when a U wave follows the T wave.

The ECG is a rough guide to potassium. A normal tracing does not mean a normal level. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]

Low at 1.5. A low magnesium often travels with a low potassium after vomiting and diarrhea, and it makes the potassium harder to correct. The consensus report does not discuss magnesium. This is general teaching on hypokalemia. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]

Normal on arrival, as it usually is, and expected to fall with insulin. The consensus report advises against routine phosphate replacement and considers it when the level is low with muscle weakness or respiratory or cardiac compromise. The report prints the cutoff as under 1.0 mmol/L. Older guidance used 1.0 mg/dL. Check your own protocol. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]

A white count of 13 is common in ketoacidosis without infection. It is a stress response and does not on its own mean she needs antibiotics. Her hemoglobin is at the top of her range from dehydration. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]

Normal. Lipase is often raised in ketoacidosis without pancreatitis, sometimes several times the upper limit, so a raised one would have needed interpreting with the abdomen. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]
Normal. Her acidosis is ketones. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]

At the top of the normal range. A high osmolality with a very high glucose and little ketosis would be the hyperosmolar state, which she does not have. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]
Clear. Pneumonia is a common trigger and she has no cough, so this was optional. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory, no source opened]

case_actions.debrief_note:
This is the step that makes the case. Her potassium was 3.1 before any insulin. Insulin moves potassium into cells, and a level that is already low falls to one that can stop the heart or the breathing muscles.

The rule by level:

Under 3.5: hold insulin. Intravenous potassium chloride at 20 to 40 mEq an hour, on a monitor. Recheck the level every one to two hours. Start insulin only once it is 3.5 or more.

3.5 to 5.5: 20 to 30 mEq of potassium in each liter of fluid, and insulin can start at the same time.

Over 5.5: hold the potassium, start insulin, and recheck in one to two hours. Insulin and fluid bring it down fast.

Rates of 20 mEq an hour and above usually mean a central line or two peripheral lines, and always a monitor. Follow your own policy. Potassium is never given as a push.

Sources differ on the numbers. The 2024 consensus report, as read for this case, gave a lower starting rate, and the 2009 American Diabetes Association statement used 3.3 as the threshold, which many hospital protocols still do. This case uses 3.5 and 20 to 40 mEq an hour, from the reference the directing physician set on 7 October 2026.

The simulator compresses hours of infusion into twenty seconds and does not model the dose. [Potassium rule from the reference table supplied by the directing physician, 7 October 2026] [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool] [UNVERIFIED: the 2009 threshold of 3.3 and the line requirements are from memory]

The simulator gives the oral dose no effect at any point in the case, which is a simplification once her vomiting has settled. Not scored. A low magnesium makes the kidneys waste potassium, so replacing it helps the potassium hold. It also protects against the rhythm problems of a long QT. Stopping insulin in a patient who is responding is the opposite mistake. A glucose that looks better is not the end point. Resolution in the consensus report is ketones under 0.6 mmol/L with a pH of 7.3 or a bicarbonate of 18 or more, and many hospitals also use a closed anion gap. case_actions.debrief_note:
She skipped her basal insulin, and that is why she is here. Giving it back is part of the treatment. The consensus report says a regimen the patient was already on 'can be continued at the usual dose', and that basal insulin 'should be started 1-2 h before cessation of intravenous insulin'.

How early to give it is not settled. The report says many clinicians give basal insulin during the infusion and others avoid it because of the risk of a low glucose or a low potassium, and that several studies of a low dose found a shorter time to resolution and less rebound hyperglycemia.

This case counts it once insulin is running and the potassium is 3.5 or more, and does not score it before then. authoring_notes.near_the_10_4_line: Two answers sit close to the limits in authoring 8.4 and are flagged for the reviewer. The diabetes topic says 'they said my blood had gone acidic' about her admission at age eleven. That is her own past history in lay words, and she does not connect it to today. The sugar topic quotes her home meter, 380 and 290. Those are numbers she read herself, not results from this visit. A reviewer may prefer either softened.

interview.volunteers_note: Hand-written for this pack. Her diabetes, her insulin doses, her sugar readings and her thirst are never volunteered.

correct_disposition.label: Step-down or intermediate care with telemetry
correct_disposition.explanation:
She needs hourly glucose checks, an insulin regimen that is being adjusted, intravenous potassium and a monitor. A step-down or intermediate unit does all of that.

The grade of ketoacidosis is not what puts her there. The 2024 consensus report suggests a regular or observation unit for mild ketoacidosis, and says the level of care is a clinical decision. Her potassium of 3.1 and the intravenous replacement on a monitor are what make step-down the better fit.

What the receiving team needs: the potassium before and after replacement, when insulin started and by which route, the plan for dextrose when the glucose is under 250, and that she reduced and then stopped her own insulin because she was not eating. She needs her long-acting insulin restarted, and sick-day teaching before she goes home: basal insulin is not stopped during illness, even when not eating, and ketones are checked.

alternative_dispositions.label: Intensive care unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: Safe, and more than she needs. She is alert with mild ketoacidosis. Some hospitals send every insulin infusion to intensive care, and in those hospitals this is the right answer.

alternative_dispositions.label: General medical ward with telemetry
alternative_dispositions.explanation: The consensus report suggests a regular unit for mild ketoacidosis, so this is defensible where the unit can check a glucose every hour, run intravenous potassium on a monitor and follow a subcutaneous insulin protocol. Many cannot, and her potassium is the reason to ask.

alternative_dispositions.label: Emergency department observation unit
alternative_dispositions.explanation: The consensus report lists an observation unit for mild ketoacidosis, and some departments run a subcutaneous insulin protocol there. A potassium that started at 3.1 and needs intravenous replacement on a monitor makes her a poor fit unless the unit is set up for it.

alternative_dispositions.label: Discharge home
alternative_dispositions.explanation: She is still in ketoacidosis. It takes hours of insulin for the ketones to clear, and she cannot yet keep fluid down. This is the outcome the triage story leads to if nobody checks a sugar.

alternative_dispositions.label: Transfer to another hospital
alternative_dispositions.explanation: This hospital has everything she needs.

correct_diagnosis.label: Diabetic ketoacidosis
correct_diagnosis.explanation:
A glucose of 348, blood ketones of 4.2 mmol/L and a pH of 7.27 with a bicarbonate of 16 in a patient with type 1 diabetes. All three parts of the definition are present. With a pH above 7.25, a bicarbonate of 15 to 18 and a clear head it is mild.

Mild describes the acidosis. It does not describe the risk. Her potassium was low before treatment, and the usual first drug would have made it dangerous.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hypokalemia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: The finding that changed the order of treatment. The receiving team needs to know it was 3.1 on arrival, because insulin will keep pushing it down and it needs checking every one to two hours while it is being replaced.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hypomagnesemia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: A low magnesium makes a low potassium harder to correct. Worth naming so it is replaced and rechecked.

additional_diagnoses.label: Viral gastroenteritis
additional_diagnoses.explanation: The trigger. Naming it tells the next team that the search for a cause was made and that no other source was found on examination or in the urine.

additional_diagnoses.label: Hypovolemia
additional_diagnoses.explanation: She was dry from vomiting, diarrhea and the glucose in her urine. True, and treated with the first fluid.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Viral gastroenteritis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She has it, and as the main diagnosis it stops one step short. Gastroenteritis explains the vomiting. It does not explain a glucose of 348, deep breathing or a bicarbonate of 16. This is the diagnosis that sends her home. Name it beside the ketoacidosis as the trigger.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Infectious gastroenteritis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: The trigger and not the problem that needs a hospital bed. The glucose, the ketones and the gas make the diagnosis.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hypokalemia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: True, and the most dangerous number she has. It is a complication. The diagnosis that explains the admission is the ketoacidosis. Name this beside it.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hyponatremia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her measured sodium was 133 at a glucose of 348. Corrected for the glucose, by adding 1.6 to 2.4 for every 100 mg/dL above 100, it is about 137 to 139, which is normal. Glucose draws water into the blood and dilutes the sodium, and the number rises on its own as the glucose falls. Report the corrected value, and expect the measured one to climb.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute kidney injury
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her creatinine was 1.2 with a BUN of 24, in a woman who was dry, and no earlier value is known. A single creatinine does not meet the definition of acute kidney injury, which needs a rise against a baseline or a fall in urine output. The likely reading is a kidney short of volume, and the handover is to repeat the creatinine after fluid.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Anion gap metabolic acidosis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Correct as a description of the gas and the chemistry. With a high glucose and ketones of 4.2 the cause is known, and the handover should say it.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hypovolemia
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: True and incomplete. Fluid alone left her bicarbonate and anion gap where they were.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: That is a much higher glucose and osmolality with little ketosis, usually in an older patient with type 2 diabetes. Her glucose is 348, her osmolality is normal and her ketones are high.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Alcoholic ketoacidosis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Ketoacidosis after heavy drinking and poor intake, usually with a normal or low glucose. She drinks little, had none this week, and has type 1 diabetes with a glucose of 348.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute pancreatitis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Worth a thought with vomiting and abdominal pain, and it can trigger ketoacidosis. Her pain is crampy and diffuse, her abdomen is soft and her lipase is normal.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Acute appendicitis
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her appendix was removed when she was fifteen, and her abdomen has no localized tenderness.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Hyperemesis gravidarum
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: Her pregnancy test is negative. It was right to check.

alternative_diagnoses.label: Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome
alternative_diagnoses.explanation: She does not use cannabis, and it does not cause a high glucose with ketones.

debrief_configuration.key_exams_note: Every exam is tagged neutral, so the Physical score reads this list: the deep breathing, the perfusion, the dry mouth, the abdomen and the mental state. Model judgment.
debrief_configuration.intended_path_note: Fluid, the chemistry, potassium, a repeat level, then insulin. A learner who gives rapid insulin at any point before the potassium has run in passes through potassium_falling and recovering and reaches the same end.
cross_cutting_teaching_points: Know the potassium before you give insulin. Under 3.5, hold insulin and replace it at 20 to 40 mEq an hour, rechecking every one to two hours, and start insulin once the level is 3.5 or more. Between 3.5 and 5.5, insulin runs with 20 to 30 mEq of potassium in each liter. Over 5.5, hold the potassium and start insulin. Insulin, bicarbonate and fluid all push potassium down. [Potassium rule from the reference table supplied by the directing physician, 7 October 2026] [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]
A vomiting adult who looks dry or is breathing deeply gets a bedside glucose. Ketoacidosis often arrives looking like a stomach bug.

Fluid treats the dehydration and insulin treats the ketoacidosis. When the glucose falls under 250, add dextrose and keep the insulin going until the ketones clear. [UNVERIFIED: Umpierrez et al. 2024, read through a summarizing tool]
Mild describes the pH. It does not describe the risk. The most dangerous number in this patient was not the glucose.

Patients who stop eating often stop their insulin. In type 1 diabetes basal insulin is not stopped during illness, even when not eating, and that teaching is part of the discharge. [UNVERIFIED: general teaching written by a model from memory]
The simulator compresses hours into seconds and does not model doses. The order of the steps is the lesson, and the timings are not.
